one_line: Panel on intent-based runtime authorization for agents: per-call authz with mission context, budgets instead of rate limits, and enforcement outside the agent. Core claim: coarse OAuth scopes don't fit autonomous agents.
summary: A Keycard-moderated panel with Keycard's CEO Ian, JPMorgan Chase's Global Chief Security Architect Michael Davis, and OAuth co-creator Dick Hardt on why agents need runtime, per-tool-call authorization instead of standing access. They argue that OAuth scopes were built for website-to-website delegation and are too coarse for agents, and that enterprises are onboarding agents gradually, the way they onboard developers. The proposed primitives are a "mission" that carries user or business intent through every decision and into the audit trail, a separate supervising agent that approves or denies the worker's actions, and layered policy where deterministic must-never rules sit under an intent-derived bounding box. Dick describes budgets as a time-limited, resource-limited grant the agent can see and that a supervisor can top up, in contrast to rate limits that cut it off silently. The brains-vs-hands pattern (credentials and API keys outside the sandboxed model, with enforcement at an egress proxy) and dynamic tool removal are offered as concrete mitigations. The panel closes on whether the risk is real, with sharply differing takes. Much of the content is conceptual and opinionated; the concrete engineering patterns are few and brief.

key_ideas.idea: Runtime authorization per tool call beats standing access
key_ideas.detail: Agents should be authorized at each tool call rather than holding broad standing access they will eventually misuse. Coarse-grained MCP tools and APIs make even the 'is this tool call allowed' question hard.

key_ideas.idea: OAuth scopes are too coarse for agents
key_ideas.detail: OAuth was built for one website letting another talk to it, with pre-registration and a redirect. Scopes were added later, but mapping them onto agents is far too coarse, because agents discover what they need over time and different instances need different things.

key_ideas.idea: Mission as the unit of context for every decision
key_ideas.detail: The user or organization gives the agent a mission. Each authorization decision is made in that context, and the mission identifier propagates through all events so an audit can reconstruct everything done under one mission. A supervising agent that cannot do the work decides what the worker may do.

key_ideas.idea: Two layers of intent: deterministic policy plus intersected intent
key_ideas.detail: Ian suggests deterministic policy for must-never actions and always-human-approval cases, then layering interactional intent (user to agent) and business intent (why the org adopted the agent). Intersecting these yields a bounding box of allowed actions, which reduces consent fatigue.

key_ideas.idea: Agents arriving at the web are an unregistered-client problem
key_ideas.detail: Ian frames agent identity as the same problem as guest checkout or CAPTCHAs: a downstream resource needs to decide whether to trust an unknown agent. He cites Vercel being blocked in Spain because of shared IP addresses as an example of how blunt blocking hurts bystanders.

key_ideas.idea: Budgets with feedback instead of rate limits
key_ideas.detail: Dick describes giving the agent a time-limited token with a resource budget. The agent sees consumption and remaining budget and can plan around scarcity. When it runs out, a supervisor decides whether to add more, while a rate limit just cuts it off with no explanation.

key_ideas.idea: Brains vs hands: keep credentials outside the model's sandbox
key_ideas.detail: The model and planning live in a sandbox that holds no API keys or broad standing access. Tools call out through an egress proxy outside the sandbox, where authorization is enforced. The panel says this pattern is what major labs are converging on, and that it keeps experimentation free while the enforcement stays deterministic.

key_ideas.idea: Memory can bias the brain; dynamically remove tools by state
key_ideas.detail: Poisoned or biased memory can push the model toward actions it shouldn't take, so separation alone isn't enough. The panel suggests removing tools dynamically based on state, for example disabling external egress tools until a required email step completes, which also reduces context bloat.

key_ideas.idea: Audit log must sit outside the agent's control
key_ideas.detail: Ian argues the enforcement point and the record of who told the agent to do what, and why, must be outside the agent so it can't tamper with them. He ties this to liability: whoever employs the agent is liable, so the audit must answer who did what.

techniques.name: Budget-as-token grant with live feedback
techniques.how: Issue a time-limited credential that also carries a resource budget. Report consumption back to the agent so it can pace itself. On exhaustion, route to a supervisor for a top-up decision instead of a hard cutoff.
techniques.when: Agents that might hammer a downstream API (e.g. a booking site) and where a human or supervisor should decide on extra quota.

techniques.name: Brains/hands split with egress-proxy enforcement
techniques.how: Run the model and planning in a sandbox with no API keys. Route all tool egress through a proxy outside the sandbox, where authorization, logging, and translation happen.
techniques.when: Any production agent that executes actions with real credentials; use it to make the enforcement point unreachable by the agent.

techniques.name: Separate supervising agent for worker actions
techniques.how: A second agent, which does no work itself, reviews the worker's requested actions against the mission and approves or denies them. Deterministic policy handles clear cases first; the supervisor handles vague ones.
techniques.when: Requests that are ambiguous (e.g. forwarding an executive's email externally) where a fixed rule is too brittle.

techniques.name: Deterministic must-never policy plus intent-derived bounds
techniques.how: Write fixed rules for actions that must never happen or always need a human. Layer user and business intent on top to compute the allowed set for a specific task, then intersect them.
techniques.when: Reducing human-approval prompts (consent fatigue) without loosening the hard limits.

techniques.name: Dynamic tool gating by task phase
techniques.how: Remove or re-enable tools based on the current step of the mission, e.g. block external web or egress tools while a sensitive write step is in progress.
techniques.when: Long-running agents with mixed read and write tools, or when context bloat from unused tools is a problem.

techniques.name: Intent and environment in trace spans
techniques.how: Attach the mission or intent identifier and environment signals (location, time, system patch state) to each span so a trace shows what the agent was doing and under what conditions.
techniques.when: Forensics or debugging of agent actions, and building audit trails that can be correlated across systems.

numbers.claim: Resy incident: an agent made 200 API calls per hour on a restaurant booking site and got the user's account banned.
Salesforce's OAuth had a single API scope for a long time, which the speaker calls unhelpful for agents.
Vercel was blocked in Spain about 2-3 years earlier because one hosted site on shared IPs was accused of illegal content.
Ian describes three levels of software factory: human-driven, workflow-driven, and agent-driven, with runtime authorization needed at all of them.

hot_takes: OAuth scopes mapped onto agents are far too coarse-grained for what agents do (Dick Hardt).
Human-in-the-loop is somewhat of an anti-pattern because of approval fatigue; bring humans in only when it matters (Michael Davis).
Guardrails decided by the agent vendor are not acceptable; the supervising policy should be independent and pluggable through a protocol (Dick Hardt).
The probability the world ends from agents is approaching zero, and agents can simply be unplugged (Ian).
More agent-specific regulation is unnecessary; existing liability law already answers who is responsible (Ian).
Coding agents and proprietary closed-box agent systems will lose to federated, interoperable protocols, and vendor-biased standards are a risk to the web (Ian and Dick).

relevance.why: Govrix Scout already has budgets and a Merkle audit log. The budget-with-feedback and supervisor-approval patterns from the talk are a direct design input for how budgets behave at the proxy.
relevance.action: Change the budget enforcement at the proxy so the agent receives remaining-budget info in responses (or headers) and an escalation path, instead of a hard 429 cutoff. Log mission or intent ID on each audited request.

relevance.why: The brains/hands split with an egress proxy matches the Scout proxy design. The talk's point is that the proxy is the enforcement boundary the agent can't reach.
relevance.action: Write down the threat model that assumes the agent holds no API keys and all tool egress goes through Scout; check which L2C Crucible or tool paths bypass the proxy.

relevance.why: The supervisor pattern (separate agent approves worker actions) and budgeted runs are close to ProsHarness's plan→critique→debate and checkpoint/resume features around the Claude Code CLI.
relevance.action: Give each ProsHarness run an explicit token/tool-call budget that the agent can see, with a checkpoint-and-ask escalation when it is exhausted instead of killing the run.

relevance.why: Dynamic tool removal by task phase is relevant to controlling Claude Code tool access during long runs, but the talk gives only a sketch.
relevance.action: Try gating which tools are exposed to the CLI per loop stage (e.g. no network egress during write steps) and measure the effect on token use.

relevance.why: Mostly conceptual panel. Useful vocabulary for threat modeling and talking to security teams, but few concrete implementations.
